title: Computational Complexity of Counting Eulerian Circuits
description: Surveys the computational complexity of counting Eulerian circuits. Decision is trivial (Euler's criterion), but counting is #P-complete for undirected graphs (Brightwell-Winkler 2005). For directed graphs, the BEST theorem gives a polynomial formula via the matrix tree theorem.

meta.author: BEST (1951), Brightwell-Winkler (2005)

meta.assumptions: No axioms, no sorries. Results are stated as documented facts (True) since #P-completeness and BEST theorem require Turing machine formalization beyond current scope.

overview.historicalContext:
**From Euler to #P-completeness**

Euler (1736) solved the Königsberg bridges problem by showing Eulerian circuits require even degrees. Hierholzer (1873) gave an efficient algorithm to find them. The BEST theorem (de Bruijn, van Aardenne-Ehrenfest, Smith, Tutte, 1951) gave an exact formula for counting directed Eulerian circuits. Brightwell and Winkler (2005) proved the surprising result that counting undirected Eulerian circuits is #P-complete.
overview.problemStatement:
**Question**: What is the computational complexity of counting Eulerian circuits?

**Answer**: Decision is O(|V|), finding is O(|E|), but counting is #P-complete for undirected graphs. For directed graphs, the BEST theorem gives polynomial counting via the matrix tree theorem.
overview.text: The complexity of counting Eulerian circuits exhibits a remarkable gap: trivial to decide, polynomial to find, but #P-complete to count in the undirected case.
overview.proofStrategy: Survey approach: state Euler's decidable criterion, document the BEST theorem formula, record the #P-completeness result, and provide concrete examples.
keyInsights: **Decision-counting gap**: Existence is trivial (check degrees), but counting is as hard as counting SAT solutions.
**Directed vs undirected gap**: Counting directed Eulerian circuits is polynomial (BEST theorem), but undirected is #P-complete.
**BEST formula**: EC(G) = t_w(G) · ∏(deg⁺(v)-1)! reduces to a single determinant computation.
**Matrix tree theorem connection**: The arborescence count t_w(G) is computed via the Laplacian matrix cofactor.

sections.title: Euler's Criterion (Decision is Easy)
sections.summary: Euler's criterion for Eulerian circuits (all even degrees) is decidable in O(|V|) time.
sections.mathContext: A connected graph has an Eulerian circuit iff every vertex has even degree. This is trivially checkable.

sections.title: The BEST Theorem
sections.summary: The BEST theorem gives a formula for counting directed Eulerian circuits: $\text{EC}(G) = t_w(G) \cdot \prod_{v} (\deg^+(v) - 1)!$.
sections.mathContext: The formula combines the arborescence count (from the matrix tree theorem) with a product of degree factorials. This yields polynomial-time counting for directed graphs.

sections.title: Complexity Results
sections.summary: Counting undirected Eulerian circuits is #P-complete (Brightwell-Winkler 2005). This is one of the most striking decision-counting gaps in combinatorics.
sections.mathContext: #P is the class of counting problems associated with NP decision problems. #P-completeness means the counting problem is at least as hard as any problem in #P.

crossReferences.description: Extends the Königsberg bridges problem from existence to counting: how many Eulerian circuits exist?

conclusion.summary: Counting Eulerian circuits reveals a dramatic complexity gap: decision is trivial (O(|V|)), but counting is #P-complete for undirected graphs. The BEST theorem gives polynomial counting for directed graphs via the matrix tree theorem.
conclusion.implications: The decision-counting gap for Eulerian circuits parallels similar gaps elsewhere (e.g., 2-coloring vs counting 2-colorings). Formalizing #P-completeness in Lean would require Turing machine infrastructure.
